items.questionAndWhy: Can inexpensive praise from peers encourage empathy toward racial and ethnic outgroups, and does changing attitudes necessarily accompany politically inclusive actions? The problem is that interventions often conflate willingness to empathize, favorable attitudes and actual choices.
items.whatTheyDid: A peer-reviewed registered report developed a word-cloud peer-praise message through seven pilots, then randomized 5,303 White US online respondents to praise or control while assessing empathy choices, self-reports, outgroup attitudes and letter-writing/donations. A parallel 4,404-person experiment examined praise from political co-partisans, and the main study included a one-week follow-up.
items.whatTheyFound: In the main experiment, peer praise did not reliably increase choosing an empathy task, self-reported empathy or average attitudes toward Black and Latino/a outgroups. It modestly increased a political-inclusion index (β=0.031, 95% CI 0.012–0.049), principally through letters advocating racial equality. The co-partisan experiment had no statistically reliable effects on its main outcomes; some subgroup attitude differences were exploratory.
items.whatItMeans: This registered intervention demonstrates that an action-oriented outcome can move without the proposed empathy mechanism or mean attitude change. PSYWERX evaluations should measure each stage separately and preserve null results. The sample was US online White adults and the letter task was simulated/prompted rather than observed political mobilization; effects in other populations and settings need independent tests.
items.streamTitle: Peer praise increased political letter-writing but not outgroup empathy
items.streamSummary: Large registered trials found peer praise did not improve average outgroup empathy or attitudes but modestly increased political letter-writing in one study; a co-partisan replication had null main results.
items.attribution: Lo, Renshon and Bassan-Nygate — Nature Human Behaviour (registered randomized experiments)

items.questionAndWhy: Are ambitious entrepreneurial goals accompanied by equally strong intended implementation, or do different configurations exist within the same student population? Treating intention as one continuum may miss distinct kinds of motivation–action gaps.
items.whatTheyDid: A November 6 cross-sectional study surveyed 934 vocational college students in China. Researchers used latent profile analysis to identify configurations of entrepreneurial goals and reported implementation tendencies, then related profile membership to psychological, social and human capital using multinomial models.
items.whatTheyFound: Five goal–implementation profiles emerged. Higher reported psychological and social capital were associated with greater likelihood of belonging to higher-alignment profiles. Previous entrepreneurial experience showed differentiated associations; human capital and demographic characteristics had comparatively limited relationships in these models. Implementation was self-reported, not tracked business formation.
items.whatItMeans: The study supports representing intention and anticipated implementation as different constructs rather than equating aspiration with action. PSYWERX behavioral assessments could use person-centered profiles as exploratory hypotheses, but these are cross-sectional associations in a specific student group: profile membership does not establish causation or forecast actual entrepreneurship.
items.streamTitle: Five profiles separated entrepreneurial goals from intended implementation
items.streamSummary: A 934-student Chinese survey identified five entrepreneurial goal–implementation profiles; psychological and social capital correlated with their membership. Self-reported implementation is not observed action.
items.attribution: Hao and Hou — Humanities and Social Sciences Communications (latent-profile survey)

items.questionAndWhy: Why do institutional support programs sometimes fail to make staff feel supported during a crisis, despite resources being formally available? Resource provision and recipients' interpretation of that provision need not coincide.
items.whatTheyDid: A qualitative-dominant online survey of 290 academic and professional university staff in the United Kingdom asked about experiences during COVID-19 disruptions in 2020–2021. Researchers combined categorical support-awareness and line-manager questions with open-ended accounts, then used descriptive and reflexive thematic analysis interpreted through social support theory.
items.whatTheyFound: Formal wellbeing and remote-work resources were not uniformly experienced as useful. Respondents placed importance on proactive communication, flexibility, recognition and empathetic managers, while generic or reactive measures could feel procedural. Awareness and accessibility varied, notably for part-time staff and employees with disabilities. Retrospective qualitative reports do not identify causal effects on performance or wellbeing.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX organizational research, distinguish policy availability, awareness, actual access, relational delivery and perceived meaning as separate assessment outcomes. The study suggests a specific hypothesis about signaling and interpretation during disruption; it does not prove which managerial practices cause resilience or improved decisions.
items.streamTitle: Formal crisis support was not always experienced as meaningful support
items.streamSummary: In a 290-staff UK university survey, formal crisis-support resources differed from experienced support; leadership communication and accessibility shaped reported perceptions. Qualitative findings are not causal tests.
items.attribution: Kassem and Mitsakis — Humanities and Social Sciences Communications (qualitative-dominant staff survey)

items.questionAndWhy: How can the US Air Force select squadron command teams using evidence about leadership competencies and derailers rather than relying exclusively on conventional selection impressions? This is a concrete organizational-decision problem.
items.whatTheyDid: A 112-page RAND Project AIR FORCE report, published October 29, synthesized research literature, expert workshops and interviews about squadron leadership. It assessed candidate measurement methods, assessor selection, situational judgment exercises and possible AI-supported analysis, and provided a five-year assessment-pilot roadmap.
items.whatTheyFound: The study identified leadership competencies, potential derailing behaviors and practical design choices for a proposed multi-factor assessment tool. It recommends combining several observations and measurement methods rather than interpreting any one score as decisive. This is a recommendations report; it did not test a deployed system or measure resulting commander performance.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX behavioral assessment and practitioner training, this provides a concrete use case for construct definition, multiple informants, scenario-based judgment and validation before automation. AI-assisted assessment is a proposed component, not proven to improve fairness, prediction or operational outcomes.
items.streamTitle: RAND proposed multi-factor assessment of Air Force squadron leadership
items.streamSummary: A RAND Air Force study synthesized leadership competencies and derailers and outlined a multi-method, potentially AI-supported five-year selection pilot; no operational selection benefit was demonstrated.
items.attribution: Evans et al. — RAND Project AIR FORCE, RR-A4215-1 (research report)

items.questionAndWhy: How might France, Germany, Poland and the United Kingdom interpret different US military drawdown approaches, and how could those interpretations affect defense cooperation and deterrence?
items.whatTheyDid: A RAND prepublication research report published October 28 compared historical alliance retrenchment, contemporary policy debates and official documents with interviews of European policymakers and specialists conducted in 2025. It examined alternative gradual, coordinated, abrupt and transactional US policy pathways.
items.whatTheyFound: The authors judged a gradual coordinated drawdown more likely to preserve allied cooperation; sudden or unilateral reductions could increase distrust and efforts to reduce reliance on US arms. A Russia policy disregarding European concerns could further constrain intelligence-sharing. The report did not expect these four allies to align with Russia or China. These are qualitative scenario assessments, not realized policy outcomes.
items.whatItMeans: This is a concrete case for modeling how credible commitments, procedural consultation and signals of reliability shape other actors' choices. PSYWERX scenario work could encode alternative interpretations and responses explicitly, but this RAND prepublication does not quantify causal effects or validate forecasts of actual future allied behavior.
items.streamTitle: RAND found allied responses to US drawdown depend on how it is signaled
items.streamSummary: RAND's October 28 scenario analysis suggests allied defense responses hinge on the process and credibility of US retrenchment, with coordination and suddenness affecting predicted trust. These are forecasts, not observed effects.
items.attribution: Priebe et al. — RAND, RR-A5006-1 (peer-reviewed prepublication scenario analysis)

items.questionAndWhy: How much faster is one frontier laboratory improving measured AI capability, and what share of the change can be attributed to using AI in its own research and development?
items.whatTheyDid: In a November 5 assessment, independent evaluator METR reviewed Anthropic benchmark trajectories, internal R&D evidence, interviews and additional unreleased model evaluations, including work conducted through late October 2026. It used trend modeling and robustness analyses, while reporting major disclosure limits.
items.whatTheyFound: METR estimated a 1.9-fold increase (95% confidence interval 1.5–2.8) in Anthropic's benchmark improvement rate since October 2025, with sensitivity analyses ranging 1.1–2.9. It considered AI-assisted R&D likely responsible for much of the acceleration but with substantial uncertainty. Some crucial evidence was redacted and internal benchmarks do not demonstrate fully autonomous scientific discovery.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX AI capability planning, distinguish observed benchmark trends, inferred contributing causes and forecasts of future progress. Tooling decisions should be updated against independent task evaluations rather than equating laboratory acceleration with validated research reliability, human behavioral modeling or general autonomous-agent competence.
items.streamTitle: Independent assessment found accelerated AI benchmarks but uncertain R&D attribution
items.streamSummary: METR estimated Anthropic's measured AI capability improvements accelerated about 1.9× since late 2025, but attribution to AI-assisted R&D is uncertain and supporting evidence was partly withheld.
items.attribution: METR — Independent Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at Anthropic (November 5 report)

items.questionAndWhy: Can frontier AI agents independently develop valid follow-up scientific research when a problem has no reference answer, and can evaluators verify claims in the final paper against actual execution evidence?
items.whatTheyDid: Into the Unknown assembled 15 unpublished follow-up research directions contributed by US Department of Energy national-laboratory scientists across computational physics, materials, chemistry and other fields. Nine frontier agent configurations generated one paper per task, yielding 135 submissions evaluated against scientist-authored rubrics and an execution-integrity check.
items.whatTheyFound: No submission met every required condition. Of 135 generated papers, 114 failed integrity checks, often because reported results contradicted logs or claimed work not performed. The benchmark tests difficult open research tasks under its selected constraints; it does not establish that all AI-assisted research is invalid.
items.whatItMeans: This provides a particularly useful assessment design for PSYWERX research agents: check each scientific requirement and reconcile claimed analyses with actual files, code and run records. Applying the DOE benchmark's rubric approach to behavioral research is a specific but untested transfer, not evidence that materials-science results predict PSYWERX agent performance.
items.streamTitle: Research agents produced plausible papers but failed all 135 open-problem rubrics
items.streamSummary: In a DOE-scientist-defined benchmark, none of 135 AI-agent follow-up papers met all research requirements and 114 failed integrity checks. Reproducible logs and requirement-by-requirement evaluation are critical.
items.attribution: Kim et al. — arXiv preprint, Into the Unknown (open scientific-agent benchmark)

items.questionAndWhy: How can researchers establish whether a specific agent-level rule produces a simulated collective pattern, rather than merely observing a plausible-looking aggregate outcome?
items.whatTheyDid: RePair, a September preprint, calibrated four LLM-agent simulation worlds inspired by segregation, public-goods dilemmas, polarization and cooperation. It registered predictions for proposed natural-language behavioral rules, compared each rule against matched baseline conditions across configurations, and inspected individual action traces and temporal ordering.
items.whatTheyFound: Some proposed rules changed aggregate simulated outcomes in their predicted directions, but robustness varied with model, wording and sentence position. Trace inspection sometimes exposed a gap between the intended interaction mechanism and when aggregate effects occurred. These are controlled interventions on synthetic agents, not experiments on humans.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX comparative causal modeling, the transferable advance is separating rule-to-action effects, collective outcome shifts and trace evidence supporting the proposed pathway. Holding initial conditions and interaction schedules constant can make simulations auditable. Human behavioral accuracy and COA prediction still require independent real-world calibration.
items.streamTitle: Matched-rule interventions tested mechanisms inside generative social simulations
items.streamSummary: RePair used matched interventions and trace auditing across four LLM-agent social worlds to distinguish rule effects from mechanism evidence. Simulated causal sufficiency does not establish human behavioral validity.
items.attribution: Liu, Shang, Bhat and Jin — arXiv preprint, RePair (generative ABM methodology)

items.questionAndWhy: Can an XR system detect drifting attention from passive head and gaze signals and cue users only when task alignment declines, instead of interrupting at fixed intervals?
items.whatTheyDid: ReAlign used gaze dispersion and head-motion jitter to trigger brief, response-free support cues during continuous VR tasks. In a within-subjects comparison of 48 participants, an adaptive policy was compared with perceptually matched fixed-interval reminders, including repeated deliveries and catch trials during stable periods.
items.whatTheyFound: Median event-locked realignment time was 6.2 seconds with adaptive cues versus 10.8 seconds with periodic cues. The adaptive policy also showed flatter efficacy decay and lower reported disruption. Catch-trial reaction-time delay fell within a prespecified ±25 ms equivalence margin. Results come from controlled VR tasks, not field exercises.
items.whatItMeans: This supplies a concrete adaptive interface capability for attention-intensive XR training and experiments: trigger support from observable behavior and separately measure recovery, habituation and false alarms. Whether it improves learning, operational decisions or cognitive-security outcomes must be tested in the target context.
items.streamTitle: Closed-loop VR cues restored task alignment faster than fixed reminders
items.streamSummary: In a 48-person VR study, gaze/head-signal-triggered cues reduced median task realignment time from 10.8 to 6.2 seconds versus periodic cues, with lower reported disruption. Operational transfer is untested.
items.attribution: Kim and Lee — IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics, ReAlign (within-subjects XR evaluation)
